clue.text: George Villiers resisting ranter

parts.note: a horse bucking is resisting its rider
a ham is an actor who rants and overplays

explanation.surface: A seventeenth-century courtier stands firm against a loudmouth.
explanation.walkthrough: George Villiers was the favourite of James I, created Duke of Buckingham.
explanation.definitionFit: Villiers held the dukedom, so his title stands for the man himself.

clue.text: Sculptor of Carlyle starts brilliantly on his marble

indicators.note: the starts of the four following words are taken, one letter from each

explanation.surface: A sculptor makes a brilliant beginning on his marble portrait of the historian.
explanation.walkthrough: Joseph Edgar Boehm (born Böhm in Vienna) made the Chelsea Embankment statue of Thomas Carlyle.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian sculptor Boehm, originally spelt Böhm, carved the well-known seated statue of the Scottish writer.

clue.text: Jonson's was altered

parts.note: points to the title of Ben Jonson's comedy about something that 'is Altered'

explanation.surface: Something belonging to Ben Jonson was changed.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben Jonson's early comedy is titled The Case is Altered, so the clue completes the title.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing noun in the title of the Jonson play fills the gap.

clue.text: Disorganised, chaotic Simon opposes holy images

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the noun: one who opposes holy images

indicators.note: disorganised letters are put in a new order, so the following two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A muddled man called Simon objects to icons in church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chaotic' looks like a second anagram signal but is fodder: its letters join those of SIMON.
explanation.definitionFit: An iconoclast who fights against religious pictures is called by this Greek-derived word meaning image-fighter.

clue.text: Roman jurist happy in France and America

parts.note: gai is French for cheerful
US is the abbreviation for the United States

explanation.surface: An ancient lawyer is content living in France and the States.
explanation.walkthrough: Gaius wrote the Institutes, the standard textbook of Roman law.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaius was a celebrated second-century legal writer whose Institutes survive.

clue.text: Tsarevna presented in Bolton

definitions.meaning: a daughter of the Tsar, here the youngest daughter of Nicholas II
the 1954 play adapted into English by Guy Bolton from Marcelle Maurette's French original

explanation.surface: A Russian princess appears on stage in a Lancashire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Bolton is a Lancashire town, but here it is the playwright Guy Bolton, who adapted the play about the woman claiming to be the surviving Romanov daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Romanov grand duchess gave her name to a play whose English version was written by Guy Bolton.

clue.text: Secure accommodation for minimalist

definitions.meaning: a barred enclosure that keeps an animal locked in
John ..., the American avant-garde composer of 4'33"

explanation.surface: A locked room fit for someone who wants little.
explanation.walkthrough: John Cage's silent piece 4'33" is the classic example of musical minimalism.
explanation.definitionFit: A barred enclosure secures its occupant, and the composer John Cage is a byword for spare, reduced music.

clue.text: Nothing delayed support for a job implying leadership of a Propaganda committee

definitions.text: job implying leadership of a Propaganda committee

parts.note: a post holds things up
O is the round figure zero
late means delayed

explanation.surface: A late support role in an office heading a body that spreads propaganda.
explanation.walkthrough: The Propaganda was the Vatican congregation for spreading the faith, a mission-leading office of the kind held by an apostle.
explanation.definitionFit: The office of an apostle is a post of missionary leadership, the work of the Church's Propaganda congregation.

clue.text: Live practical acquaintance with theme of Blake songs

definitions.meaning: to go through or undergo something
Blake's Songs of Innocence and of ... contrast two states of the soul

explanation.surface: Living first-hand knowledge of the subject of William Blake's poems.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means to undergo something, the knowledge gained by doing, and the second state in Blake's paired collection of songs.

clue.text: Like Sabatini's Nights

parts.note: refers to Rafael Sabatini's collection of true tales about real past events, titled with the adjective before 'Nights' Entertainment'

explanation.surface: Resembling evenings spent with a romance novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Rafael Sabatini, author of Captain Blood, also wrote The Historical Nights' Entertainment.
explanation.definitionFit: Sabatini's collection of true episodes from the past bears this adjective in its title.

clue.text: Coward seemed to associate it with detail

definitions.text: Coward seemed to associate it with detail

parts.words: Coward seemed to associate it with detail
parts.note: Noël Coward's only novel pairs this word with 'Circumstance', and circumstance can mean particular detail

explanation.surface: A timid person apparently links something to fine points.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coward' is Noël Coward, whose novel is Pomp and Circumstance; 'circumstance' in the sense of particular detail is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Ceremonial splendour is coupled with 'Circumstance' in Coward's novel title, borrowed from Othello.

clue.text: Actors with monarch on crossing in administrative centre

parts.note: the cast is the company of actors in a production
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the Queen
a bridge is a crossing over water

explanation.surface: Players with the sovereign on a bridge in a county town.
explanation.walkthrough: Hardy's Casterbridge, from The Mayor of Casterbridge, is his fictional Dorchester, the county town of Dorset.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's fictional market town stands for Dorchester, the seat of county government in his Wessex.

clue.text: Siegfried Sassoon bitterly wonders if it is significant

definitions.text: Siegfried Sassoon bitterly wonders if it is significant

parts.words: Siegfried Sassoon bitterly wonders if it is significant
parts.note: the title of Sassoon's war poem asking, in bitter irony, whether losing legs or sight is of any importance

explanation.surface: A war poet asks bitterly whether something counts.
explanation.walkthrough: Sassoon's poem repeats its title question ironically about soldiers maimed in the First World War.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's title is the question of whether something has any importance.

clue.text: Painting genre surprisingly fills islet

indicators.note: something arranged surprisingly is in an unexpected order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Painting overtakes a small island unexpectedly.
explanation.definitionFit: Pictures of fruit, flowers and objects form a recognised category of art.

clue.text: Order first name of Lara's creator

definitions.meaning: the Cistercian monks reformed by St Bernard of Clairvaux

explanation.surface: A command, and the given name of the person who wrote about Lara.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lara' suggests Byron or Doctor Zhivago, but it is Bernardine Evaristo's verse novel Lara.
explanation.definitionFit: Monks following St Bernard are a religious order, and the Booker-winning novelist Evaristo bears this forename.

clue.text: Colin McInnes's Absolute Beginners

parts.note: the 1959 novel about young people in late-1950s London youth culture

explanation.surface: A novelist's complete novices.
explanation.walkthrough: Colin MacInnes's Absolute Beginners chronicles the new youth culture of 1958 London, its young people 'beginners' at life.
explanation.definitionFit: The novel's beginners are the young people aged thirteen to nineteen of the new 1950s youth culture.

clue.text: Morse code?

parts.note: not the dots-and-dashes signal but the hidden first name of Colin Dexter's Inspector Morse

explanation.surface: The telegraph signalling system of dots and dashes.
explanation.walkthrough: Colin Dexter's detective Morse kept his first name secret, a code of sorts, until it was revealed late in the series.
explanation.definitionFit: Inspector Morse's concealed forename was eventually revealed in the novels.

clue.text: Perhaps it led a 19

definitions.note: one example of the mark named at 19-across

indicators.note: perhaps signals one possible arrangement, so the letters may be reordered

explanation.surface: Possibly it was in front.
explanation.walkthrough: The 19 is 19-across, DIACRITIC: the wavy mark over the n in Spanish is one.
explanation.definitionFit: The wavy mark used in Spanish and Portuguese is an accent placed over a letter.

clue.text: Manet and Burroughs depicted the bare fact of it

definitions.text: Manet and Burroughs depicted the bare fact of it

parts.words: Manet and Burroughs depicted the bare fact of it
parts.note: Manet's painting shows a nude woman at a picnic meal on the grass, and Burroughs wrote a novel naming that meal 'Naked'

explanation.surface: A painter and a novelist both showed the plain truth about something.
explanation.walkthrough: Manet's Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe (Luncheon on the Grass) has a nude, and William Burroughs wrote Naked Lunch; 'bare' means naked.
explanation.definitionFit: Both works feature a midday meal paired with nakedness.

clue.text: Dreadful reviewer reportedly used to modify sound

indicators.note: reportedly means as spoken, so the phrase is heard rather than read

parts.note: a dire critic is a terrible reviewer

explanation.surface: A dreadful reviewer is said to be used to change sound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dire critic' spoken runs together into a word for an accent mark, which changes how a letter is pronounced.
explanation.definitionFit: Marks such as accents and cedillas alter a letter's pronunciation.

clue.text: "Thou shalt find a king that will revenge —'s death" (Henry IV Part I)

definitions.text: "Thou shalt find a king that will revenge —'s death" (Henry IV Part I)

parts.words: "Thou shalt find a king that will revenge —'s death" (Henry IV Part I)
parts.note: Douglas, at Shrewsbury, speaks of the nobleman he has killed while he was dressed as the King

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare about avenging a death.
explanation.walkthrough: At the battle of Shrewsbury, Douglas kills Sir Walter Blunt and earlier Stafford, both disguised as King Henry.
explanation.definitionFit: The nobleman killed in the King's armour at Shrewsbury fills the gap in the quotation.

clue.text: Bogus, like Mozart's gardener

definitions.meaning: Mozart's opera La ... giardiniera, the pretend garden-girl

explanation.surface: A fake, like the gardener in a Mozart opera.
explanation.walkthrough: In Mozart's opera La finta giardiniera a noblewoman disguises herself as a garden-girl.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian word for feigned describes the pretend gardener in Mozart's opera title.

clue.text: "The beautiful little — had nothing for it but her attractive soul-case" (H. B. Stowe, Oldtown Folks)

definitions.text: "The beautiful little — had nothing for it but her attractive soul-case" (H. B. Stowe, Oldtown Folks)

parts.words: "The beautiful little — had nothing for it but her attractive soul-case" (H. B. Stowe, Oldtown Folks)
parts.note: Stowe describes a pretty girl as a deception whose charm was all outward show

explanation.surface: A quotation from Harriet Beecher Stowe about a pretty but empty girl.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word calls the girl a deception: her looks promised what was not inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A deception or fraud, here a girl whose beauty hid nothing within, fills the gap.

clue.text: Canal flows uphill for god

indicators.note: in a down clue, going uphill means reading from bottom to top, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: the Suez Canal links the Mediterranean and the Red Sea

explanation.surface: A waterway's current runs uphill for a deity.
explanation.definitionFit: The chief of the Greek pantheon is the supreme deity.

clue.text: Just like Rosamond

definitions.meaning: Rosamond Clifford, mistress of Henry II

explanation.surface: Merely resembling a woman called Rosamond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just' looks like 'merely', but it means equitable.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means even-handed and is the epithet of Henry II's beautiful mistress Rosamond Clifford.

clue.text: She touched John Ridd with "sudden delight"

definitions.text: She touched John Ridd with "sudden delight"

parts.words: She touched John Ridd with "sudden delight"
parts.note: the heroine of R. D. Blackmore's Exmoor romance, loved by its narrator John Ridd

explanation.surface: A woman moved a young man with sudden joy.
explanation.walkthrough: John Ridd narrates Blackmore's 1869 novel set on Exmoor and loves its title heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: Blackmore's heroine is the girl John Ridd loves from boyhood in the novel named after her.

clue.text: Penman brother of Shaunn the Post

definitions.text: Penman brother of Shaunn the Post

parts.words: Penman brother of Shaunn the Post
parts.note: Joyce's Finnegans Wake has twin brothers, one a writer called 'the Penman', the other 'the Post'

explanation.surface: A writer whose brother is a postman.
explanation.walkthrough: In Finnegans Wake the twin sons of HCE are Shem the Penman and Shaun the Post.
explanation.definitionFit: Joyce's writer twin in Finnegans Wake is the brother of Shaun the postman.

clue.text: Extra rex as wayward operatic king

indicators.note: wayward means going astray, so the letters wander into a new order

explanation.surface: An extra Latin king behaves waywardly on the opera stage.
explanation.walkthrough: Arne's and others' operas take their title from the Persian king.
explanation.definitionFit: The Persian ruler is the title role of operas by Arne and many others.
